title: Segholate Nouns (Second Declension)
description: Inflect nouns like מֶלֶךְ and סֵפֶר.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Segholates like מֶלֶךְ (king) and סֵפֶר (book) are stressed on their first syllable. They are really one syllable, malk and sipr, with a helping vowel between the last two consonants; before a suffix the original form returns: מַלְכִּי (my king). The plural takes new vowels: מְלָכִים (kings).

blocks.caption: The segholates
blocks.html: A segholate looks like a two-syllable word accented on the first syllable (מֶלֶךְ, king; סֵפֶר, book; קֹדֶשׁ, holiness). It is really a monosyllable — malk, siphr, qodhsh — into which a furtive vowel (seghol) has been slipped to separate the final two consonants, which Hebrew will not pronounce together. With an inflectional addition the word returns to its monosyllabic core: מַלְכִּי (my king), סִפְרוֹ (his book). The plural takes a helping a: מְלָכִים (kings), סְפָרִים (books).

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not stress a segholate on its last syllable: מֶלֶךְ is MEH-lekh. Before a suffix it is one syllable again (מַלְכִּי), and in the plural it takes the vowels of a strong noun (מְלָכִים).
